laws.title: Drink Driving — 0.5g/L BAC Limit
laws.subtitle: Ley 24.449 — Zero tolerance in some provinces
laws.fullDescription: National limit is 0.5g/L BAC. Several provinces (Buenos Aires, Santa Fe) have zero tolerance (0.0g/L). Commercial drivers and motorcyclists face 0.2g/L limit. Police conduct sobriety checkpoints (control de alcoholemia) routinely.
laws.penalty: 0.5–1.0g/L: fine of 5–20 minimum daily wages, suspension. Above 1.0g/L: criminal charges possible.
exceptions: Zero tolerance in certain provinces overrides national limit

quiz.q: Argentina's national blood alcohol limit for drivers?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's national BAC limit is 0.5g/L, though some provinces enforce zero tolerance.

laws.title: Argentine Greetings — Cheek Kiss for Everyone
laws.subtitle: Even between men — one kiss on the right cheek
laws.fullDescription: Argentina stands out: even men greet each other with a single kiss on the right cheek (unlike most Latin America where men shake hands). This applies in Buenos Aires and most of the country. Yerba mate sharing is a gesture of deep friendship — accepting is important when offered. Dinner is late: 9–10pm is standard. Being fashionably late (30+ min) to dinner parties is normal.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — refusing the cheek kiss greeting can seem standoffish.
exceptions: More formal business settings may use handshakes
Elderly or very traditional individuals may prefer handshakes

quiz.q: What makes Argentine greeting culture unique in Latin America?
options: Men also greet each other with a cheek kiss
quiz.explanation: Unusually, even men in Argentina greet each other with a single cheek kiss — unlike most of Latin America.

laws.title: Malvinas/Falklands Sensitivity — Maps and Territorial Claims
laws.subtitle: Argentine law claims sovereignty — topic requires care
laws.fullDescription: Argentina officially claims sovereignty over the Falkland Islands (referred to as Islas Malvinas). Argentine law requires maps sold in Argentina to show the Malvinas as Argentine territory. Referring to them as the Falklands or showing them as British in any official document or product within Argentina can create legal issues. As a foreign visitor, politically engaging on this topic is strongly discouraged.
laws.penalty: Products misrepresenting territorial claims: confiscation + fines under Defensa de los Intereses de la Nación Argentina laws.
exceptions: Personal private conversations
Academic/journalistic contexts may have more latitude

quiz.q: What are the Falkland Islands called in Argentina?
quiz.explanation: Argentina calls the Falkland Islands 'Las Malvinas' and claims sovereignty — it is a deeply sensitive political topic and all official Argentine maps show them as Argentine territory.

laws.title: Yerba Mate — Sacred Social Ritual
laws.subtitle: Sharing mate is a bond; never refuse, never say gracias until done
laws.fullDescription: Yerba mate is Argentina's national drink and a social ritual with strict etiquette. The host fills the gourd (mate) and passes it to each person in sequence. You never say 'gracias' (thank you) until you're done and don't want any more — saying gracias means you're refusing further rounds. Never add sugar unless offered. Never rearrange the bombilla (metal straw). Sharing mate is an act of trust and friendship.
laws.penalty: No legal penalty — refusing mate or saying 'gracias' too early signals you want to leave the circle.
exceptions: Health reasons are universally respected
Foreigners given considerable grace for learning the ritual

quiz.q: When should you say 'gracias' when sharing yerba mate in Argentina?
options: Only when you are done and don't want any more rounds
quiz.explanation: Saying 'gracias' during a mate circle signals you are finished — don't say it until you genuinely want no more.

laws.title: Currency Exchange — Peso Inflation and Blue Dollar History
laws.subtitle: Argentina's complex foreign exchange — Official vs informal rates
laws.fullDescription: Argentina has a long history of currency crises, sovereign debt defaults, and complex exchange controls. Argentina has experienced one of the world's highest inflation rates (over 100% annually in recent years). The 'blue dollar' (parallel informal exchange rate) historically offered significantly better rates than official rates — but exchanging at this unofficial rate is technically illegal under CEDIN laws. Currently, Argentina has implemented currency unification reforms. Cash USD and euros are widely sought. Always check current BCRA (Central Bank) regulations before travel.
laws.penalty: Illegal currency exchange (black market): criminal prosecution under FX control laws. Tax evasion on undeclared foreign currency: significant fines.
exceptions: Official bank exchanges and legally licensed exchange offices
International transfers via official banking system
laws.sourceLabel: Banco Central de la República Argentina — FX Regulations

quiz.q: What was the 'blue dollar' in Argentina?
options: The official Central Bank exchange rate
An informal parallel exchange rate for USD that exceeded the official rate
A specific US banknote series preferred in Argentina
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 'blue dollar' was an informal parallel USD exchange rate that offered better rates than official channels — but exchanging at this rate is technically illegal under Argentine foreign exchange control laws.

laws.title: Patagonia Wildlife Protection — Penguin Colonies and Glaciers
laws.subtitle: Parks and Wildlife Law 22.351 — No approaching wildlife; glacier rules
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Patagonia is home to extraordinary wildlife, including Magellanic penguin colonies at Punta Tombo (the world's largest), right whales at Península Valdés (UNESCO World Heritage Site), and the Perito Moreno Glacier. Strict rules apply: tourists must stay on boardwalks at penguin colonies (minimum distances enforced by rangers), must not touch or disturb wildlife, and glacier visits require licensed guides. The Glacier Law (Ley 26.639) protects all glaciers from mining or industrial activity that could damage them.
laws.penalty: Disturbing wildlife in national parks: fines up to ARS 5 million + criminal prosecution. Approaching nesting penguins: expulsion from colony. Glacier Law violations (mining): criminal charges.
exceptions: Scientific research with National Parks Administration permit
Licensed tour operators on designated paths
Emergency situations
laws.sourceLabel: National Parks Administration Argentina — Law 22.351 and Glacier Law 26.639

quiz.q: What does Argentina's Glacier Law (Ley 26.639) protect?
options: All glaciers from mining or industrial activity that could damage them
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 2010 Glacier Law protects all glaciers and periglacial environments from mining, industrial activity, and contamination — a pioneering environmental law for South American water security.

laws.title: Ley de Medios — Media Ownership and Public Broadcasting Rules
laws.subtitle: Broadcasting Law 26.522 — Media pluralism and state media mandated
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Broadcasting Law 26.522 (the 'Ley de Medios', 2009) limits media concentration and mandates that 33% of broadcast spectrum be reserved for nonprofit organisations. The public broadcaster CONICET/RTA is required to provide universal access. Political advertising is tightly regulated during campaigns. Filming or photographing government buildings, military installations, and federal courts without authorisation is prohibited. In 2023, Argentina also introduced strict regulations on filming protests — police and security forces can restrict press access during public disorder.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized filming of federal courts or government buildings: fine + equipment confiscation. Campaign advertising violations: heavy fines per infraction.
exceptions: Accredited journalists with press credentials
Education and academic research with official authorization

quiz.q: What percentage of Argentina's broadcast spectrum must be reserved for nonprofit organisations under the 2009 Ley de Medios?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Broadcasting Law 26.522 reserves 33% of broadcast spectrum for nonprofit organisations to promote media pluralism and community broadcasting.

laws.title: Noise Ordinances — Buenos Aires Quiet Hours and Asado Smoke Rules
laws.subtitle: Ley 1540 — Noise limits; neighbourly asado smoke disputes
laws.fullDescription: Buenos Aires has a comprehensive environmental noise law (Ley 1540) that sets strict decibel limits by zone and time. Residential zones have a limit of 45dB during the day and 40dB at night — amplified music must comply. Tango milongas and live music venues in tourist areas must have soundproofing or face fines. In residential neighbourhoods, playing loud music after 10pm on weekdays or after midnight on weekends can result in police intervention. Asado (Argentine BBQ) smoke is a culturally sensitive issue — smoke that significantly affects neighbours can be reported under nuisance provisions of the Civil and Commercial Code. Buenos Aires also restricts lighting open fires on balconies or in buildings.
laws.penalty: Noise violation in residential zone: ARG $10,000–100,000 fine (inflation-adjusted). Nuisance asado smoke in apartment: civil complaint + mediation.
exceptions: Licensed live music venues with soundproofing certificates
Public festivals with municipal permits
laws.sourceLabel: Buenos Aires City Government — Ley 1540 Acoustic Pollution

quiz.q: What is the nighttime residential noise limit in Buenos Aires under Ley 1540?
quiz.explanation: Buenos Aires's Ley 1540 sets the residential nighttime noise limit at 40dB — violations can result in police intervention and fines. The law covers all noise sources including music, machinery, and commercial activities.

laws.title: Tango — UNESCO Heritage; Buenos Aires Milonga Etiquette Has Strict Codes
laws.subtitle: UNESCO Intangible Heritage 2009 — Milonga codes: cabeceo, ronda, dress rules
laws.fullDescription: Argentine tango was jointly inscribed on UNESCO's Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2009 (shared with Uruguay). The Buenos Aires milonga (tango dance hall) operates under a strict code of etiquette with real social consequences: the 'cabeceo' (subtle nod invitation) system is used to invite partners — calling out or tapping someone on the shoulder is a serious breach. Dancers move counter-clockwise in a ronda (line of dance) — cutting across the floor is extremely rude. Dress codes at traditional milongas (especially in San Telmo and Palermo) are formal: jackets for men, heels or smart shoes for women. Talking during a tanda (set of songs) is frowned upon. The MALBA cultural centre and the Centro Cultural Kirchner host regular tango events with educational programmes for visitors.
laws.penalty: No criminal law on milonga etiquette — but social enforcement is absolute. Dress code violations: refusal of entry. Ronda disruption: public censure.
exceptions: Tango practicas (practice sessions) have more relaxed codes for beginners
Tourist milongas in San Telmo adapt codes for international visitors
laws.sourceLabel: UNESCO — Tango: Intangible Cultural Heritage of Argentina and Uruguay

quiz.q: What is the name of the subtle eye-contact invitation system used in traditional Buenos Aires milongas to invite a dance partner?
quiz.explanation: The 'cabeceo' is the traditional tango invitation — a subtle raise of the eyebrows or nod across the room. The lady accepts by holding eye contact and nodding back. Calling out or approaching directly is considered impolite in traditional milongas.

laws.title: Football Fan Violence Law — Argentina's Strict Barra Brava and Stadium Safety Regulations
laws.subtitle: Argentina banned away fans in 2013 after stadium deaths; football violence laws among toughest in region
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's football (soccer) has a severe hooliganism problem — barras bravas (organized fan groups with criminal ties) have been responsible for dozens of deaths. After the 2013 death of a River Plate fan at the Belgrano match, Argentina implemented a ban on away fans at first-division matches — a ban that has been extended multiple times. The Law for the Prevention of Violence in Sporting Events (Law 24192) creates specific criminal offenses for stadium violence, imposing penalties beyond normal assault charges. Criminal sanctions target barra brava leaders, not just individual offenders. Weapons, flares, and fireworks are banned from all stadiums. National passports and DNI (national ID) are checked at entry gates with biometric systems at major stadiums. Club executives can face criminal charges if they knew of but failed to stop barra brava criminal activity.
laws.penalty: Stadium violence: up to 10 years imprisonment under Law 24192. Weapons in stadiums: 3–6 years. Club executives enabling barras: up to 6 years.
exceptions: International matches (Copa Libertadores, World Cup qualifiers) may have different arrangements
Lower division clubs with smaller barra presence may negotiate limited away fans
Police-authorized family sections with separate entry points
laws.sourceLabel: Argentina Official Gazette — Law 24192 Sporting Violence Prevention

quiz.q: What triggered Argentina's 2013 ban on away fans at first-division football matches?
options: A FIFA directive requiring enhanced safety measures
A court order following a stadium fire
The death of a River Plate fan at a match against Belgrano
A government commission report on barra brava corruption
quiz.explanation: The death of a River Plate fan at a match against Belgrano in 2013 prompted Argentina to ban away fans from first-division matches — a measure intended to reduce the violent clashes between rival barras bravas that had caused deaths at Argentine football grounds.

laws.title: Argentina's Universal Child Allowance — Conditional Cash Transfer Program Legal Framework
laws.subtitle: Argentina provides monthly payments to 4 million+ children; conditions include school attendance and vaccinations
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Universal Child Allowance (Asignación Universal por Hijo, AUH), established by Decree 1602/2009, provides monthly cash transfers to families with children under 18 who are unemployed or work in the informal economy. The program covers approximately 4 million children. It is conditional: 80% of the monthly payment is given immediately, while 20% is held back until the family certifies annual school attendance and vaccination records through ANSES (social security administration). The payment is per child (up to 5 children) and is non-means-tested within the target population. Fraudulent claims (falsifying school or vaccination records) result in benefit clawback plus fines. The AUH significantly reduced child poverty upon introduction — subsequent evaluation showed measurable impacts on education attendance and child health.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent benefit claims: repayment of all wrongfully received payments + fines up to 3x the amount received + potential criminal charges for fraud.
exceptions: Children of parents formally employed in registered economy receive Asignación Familiar (different program)
Families with income above informal economy threshold ineligible
Disabled children receive a higher disability supplement under a parallel program
laws.sourceLabel: ANSES Argentina — Universal Child Allowance Program

quiz.q: How is Argentina's Universal Child Allowance structured to ensure compliance with its education and health conditions?
options: Monthly payments are withheld until annual verification is complete
80% is paid monthly; 20% is held back until annual school/vaccination certification
Payments are made quarterly after verified attendance records
Parents must submit monthly attendance photos to ANSES
quiz.explanation: Argentina's AUH pays 80% of the monthly amount immediately, while holding back 20% until the family provides annual certification of school attendance and vaccination records through ANSES. This structure incentivizes compliance with the program's human development conditions while providing regular income support.

laws.title: Milei's Libertarian Shock Therapy
laws.subtitle: Javier Milei's 2024 'chainsaw' austerity cut state spending by 30% in months
laws.fullDescription: Javier Milei, elected December 2023 on a radical libertarian platform, enacted Argentina's most dramatic economic transformation since the 1990s. His 'chainsaw' and 'blender' approach eliminated 13 government ministries, cut real public spending by ~30% within months, eliminated fuel and transport subsidies overnight, devalued the peso 50% immediately, and abolished thousands of regulations via the Omnibus Bill and mega-DNU decrees. Monthly inflation peaked at 25% in December 2023 before falling. Poverty briefly rose above 50% before declining. The IMF praised fiscal adjustment while social protests surged. By late 2024, Argentina achieved its first fiscal surplus in 16 years.
laws.penalty: DNU (executive necessity decrees) bypassing Congress carry legal challenges. Protests blocking public roads: criminal charges under new law. State employees hired without justification face termination.
exceptions: Pension adjustments are subject to congressional override
Provincial governments retain some independent fiscal authority
IMF program conditions apply as external constraints on policy reversals

quiz.q: What was Argentina's approximate monthly inflation rate in December 2023 following Milei's immediate peso devaluation?
quiz.explanation: Following Milei's 50% peso devaluation in December 2023, monthly inflation peaked at approximately 25% — though his fiscal reforms subsequently reduced inflation significantly through 2024.

laws.title: Dollarization Debate & Peso Instability
laws.subtitle: Argentina has defaulted on its debt 9 times — Milei's dollarization proposal sparked fierce debate
laws.fullDescription: Argentina has experienced 9 sovereign debt defaults since independence — more than almost any country — and has had over 120% annual inflation in 2023. Javier Milei won the 2023 election partly on a promise to dollarize the economy: replacing the peso entirely with the US dollar, as Ecuador did in 2000. In office, Milei did not immediately dollarize due to insufficient dollar reserves but instead pursued a crawling peg devaluation strategy. The debate over dollarization cuts to the heart of Argentina's perennial economic dilemmas: without a national currency, monetary policy is impossible; with it, politicians repeatedly print money to fund deficits.
laws.penalty: Parallel dollar market (cueva/blue dollar) trading: criminal prosecution for unlicensed exchange dealers. Tax evasion through dollar accounts held abroad: AFIP enforcement with penalties up to 10x evaded amount. Capital controls violations: fines.
exceptions: Foreign-currency bank accounts (dollar savings) are legally permitted in Argentina
Export earnings must be settled at official exchange rate within set timeframe
Real estate transactions in Buenos Aires are almost universally priced in US dollars

quiz.q: How many times has Argentina defaulted on its sovereign debt since independence?
quiz.explanation: Argentina has defaulted on its sovereign debt approximately 9 times since independence — more than almost any other country — a record that has made it a case study in fiscal mismanagement and contributed to Milei's radical economic reform proposals.

laws.title: Femicide Law: Gender-Based Murder as Aggravated Homicide
laws.subtitle: Argentina's 'Ni Una Menos' movement drove landmark 2012 legislation making femicide a distinct aggravated crime
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Penal Code reform in 2012 (Law 26.791) made femicide — the killing of a woman because of her gender — an aggravated homicide carrying life imprisonment. The reform followed the 'Ni Una Menos' (Not One Less) movement, which exploded into massive street protests in 2015 after a series of high-profile gender killings. Argentina records approximately 250–300 femicides per year. The law also covers trans femicide and any killing by a person with whom the victim had a domestic relationship. Courts have increasingly applied the aggravated charge, though enforcement and conviction rates remain a subject of ongoing advocacy.
laws.penalty: Life imprisonment (prisión perpetua) — the maximum sentence under Argentine law. No parole for the first 35 years
exceptions: The law requires prosecutors to prove gender motive — 'because she was a woman' or by gender hatred
Domestic violence femicide can also trigger aggravated sentencing even without explicit gender motive proof
laws.sourceLabel: Argentina Ministry of Justice – Femicide Law

quiz.q: What famous protest slogan drove Argentina's 2015 mass mobilization against femicide?
quiz.explanation: 'Ni Una Menos' (Not One Less) became the rallying cry of Argentina's mass feminist movement against femicide, with millions marching in 2015 after a series of high-profile gender killings.

laws.title: Milei's Chainsaw Reforms: Deregulation Decree & State Dismantling
laws.subtitle: President Milei took office with a chainsaw prop and immediately issued the largest deregulation decree in Argentine history
laws.fullDescription: Javier Milei won Argentina's November 2023 presidential election on a radical libertarian platform, famously campaigning with a chainsaw symbolizing his intent to slash the state. In December 2023, he issued Decree of Necessity and Urgency (DNU) 70/2023 — deregulating or eliminating over 300 laws covering rent controls, labor protections, privatizations, and economic regulations in a single executive order. He also proposed a 664-article omnibus reform bill. Argentina's Supreme Court partially struck down the DNU's labor provisions. Milei eliminated the Ministries of Education, Health, and Women. He dollarized some sectors and achieved a fiscal surplus within months through severe austerity, dramatically cutting public wages and social spending.
laws.penalty: No new criminal penalties — these are deregulatory reforms removing existing restrictions. Some labor protections eliminated by the DNU previously had criminal enforcement mechanisms for employer violations
exceptions: The Supreme Court suspended labor market deregulation provisions of the DNU pending judicial review
Provincial governments retain jurisdiction over many areas affected by the DNU

quiz.q: What symbol did Javier Milei famously use during his 2023 presidential campaign to represent his economic reform agenda?
quiz.explanation: Milei famously campaigned wielding a chainsaw as a symbol of his intent to slash Argentina's state and government spending — then issued the largest deregulation decree in Argentine history within weeks of taking office in December 2023.

laws.title: Las Malvinas Son Argentinas: Constitutional Claim & the 1982 War
laws.subtitle: Argentina's constitution permanently claims the Falkland Islands — and the 1982 war that killed 900 people ended a military dictatorship
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's 1994 constitution includes a permanent 'Transitory Provision' claiming sovereignty over the Malvinas (Falkland Islands), South Georgia, and South Sandwich Islands — declaring their recovery 'a permanent and unrelinquishable goal.' The 1982 Falklands War began when Argentina's military junta invaded the British-controlled islands; Britain's task force retook them after 74 days of fighting, killing 649 Argentine and 255 British servicemen plus 3 Falkland Islanders. Argentina's defeat accelerated the junta's collapse and the return of democracy in 1983. The islands remain British; their residents vote overwhelmingly to remain so. Both the UK and Argentina claim the islands; UN resolutions call for negotiations.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for Argentine citizens regarding the claim — it is a constitutional and diplomatic matter
exceptions: British citizens on the islands operate under UK law and have elected their own legislative assembly
Trade and travel between Argentina and the Falklands has fluctuated with diplomatic relations
laws.sourceLabel: Argentina Ministry of Foreign Affairs – Malvinas

quiz.q: What significant political consequence did Argentina's defeat in the 1982 Falklands War have domestically?
options: It led to Argentina joining NATO
It accelerated the collapse of the military junta and the return to democracy in 1983
quiz.explanation: Argentina's military defeat in the Falklands War significantly accelerated the discrediting and collapse of the military junta, helping speed the return to democratic government in December 1983 — making the war a paradoxical catalyst for Argentina's democratic transition.

laws.title: Asado Culture Protection
laws.subtitle: Argentina's asado (BBQ) tradition has informal legal and cultural protections
laws.fullDescription: While not a formal law, Argentina's Senate in 2022 passed a declaration recognizing the asado (traditional Argentine barbecue) as an 'intangible cultural heritage of the Argentine people.' The wood-fire beef asado is central to Argentine identity — the country has the world's highest per-capita beef consumption. Argentina's export-focused cattle and beef industry is heavily regulated: export quotas, price controls (Precios Cuidados program), and beef export restrictions have been used to keep domestic prices affordable for Argentines. During periods of economic crisis, presidents have publicly promised to protect Argentines' access to affordable asado as a political priority.
laws.penalty: Violations of beef export quotas: heavy fines and export license revocation for meat-packing companies
exceptions: Premium Angus and Wagyu beef are often excluded from price controls and export quotas
Organic and artisanal producers may be exempt from standard regulatory controls

quiz.q: Which country has the world's highest per-capita beef consumption?
quiz.explanation: Argentina consistently ranks #1 globally for per-capita beef consumption, averaging approximately 50–55 kg per person per year. The asado (wood-fire barbecue) is the central cultural expression of this tradition.

laws.title: Milei's Deregulation Laws
laws.subtitle: Argentina's Javier Milei passed sweeping deregulation by decree in 2023–2024
laws.fullDescription: President Javier Milei, elected in November 2023 on a radical libertarian platform, signed the 'Megadecree' (DNU 70/2023) repealing or modifying over 300 regulations in Argentina. Changes included deregulating the real estate market (ending rent controls), liberalizing foreign currency regulations, deregulating air transport (open skies), and dismantling price controls on basic goods. The 'Omnibus Law' (partially approved by Congress in 2024) further extended deregulation. Milei closed or merged 10 government ministries and cut the public sector. Argentina's inflation — which peaked at 289% annually in 2024 — began falling by late 2024 amid severe austerity. Critics argue the shock therapy disproportionately harmed the poor.
laws.penalty: N/A — deregulation removes penalties; the decree eliminated enforcement mechanisms in many sectors
exceptions: Constitutional rights cannot be reduced by decree — some DNU provisions were challenged in court
Provincial laws and regulations are not affected by federal decrees

quiz.q: What was Argentina's peak annual inflation rate in 2024?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's annual inflation reached approximately 289% in late 2023/early 2024 — one of the highest in the world at that time — which drove voters to elect Javier Milei and his radical libertarian economic shock therapy.

laws.title: Ingreso Familiar de Emergencia (IFE) and Social Policy Framework
laws.subtitle: Argentina's emergency income transfer during COVID-19 reached 9 million households
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Ingreso Familiar de Emergencia (IFE — Emergency Family Income) was a cash transfer program launched in April 2020 at the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, providing ARS 10,000 (approximately US$150 at the time) per month to informal workers, domestic workers, and low-income earners excluded from the formal labor protection system. The IFE was paid three times in 2020 and reached approximately 9 million people — about 1 in 5 Argentines. It was administered through ANSES (National Social Security Administration) and paid via Cuenta DNI (a bank account linked to national ID). The IFE built on Argentina's existing Universal Child Allowance (AUH) and highlighted the importance of digital financial inclusion. Critics of President Milei's 2023 austerity policies expressed concern about the elimination of social transfer programs; Milei's administration sharply reduced social spending as part of fiscal consolidation efforts.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent claims for IFE or social benefits: criminal prosecution for benefit fraud under the Anti-Corruption Law
exceptions: Formal employees receiving unemployment insurance were excluded from IFE
Public employees were excluded
Those already receiving other social benefits were excluded

laws.title: Milei's 'Chainsaw' Economic Reform Package (DNU 70/2023)
laws.subtitle: Argentina's libertarian president enacted sweeping deregulation by emergency decree in 2023
laws.fullDescription: Javier Milei, elected Argentina's president in November 2023, enacted an extraordinary economic reform package on his first day in office (December 20, 2023) via Decree of Necessity and Urgency (DNU) No. 70/2023 — bypassing Congress. The 'Omnibus Decree' deregulated: rent controls (eliminating the 2020 rent freeze law); labor markets (simplifying dismissal procedures and reducing severance); foreign exchange controls (beginning devaluation to market rate — the peso was devalued 54% immediately); privatization of state companies; elimination of export quotas for agricultural products; and hundreds of regulatory modifications across sectors. Argentina's Congress challenged the DNU in courts; some provisions were struck down. Milei's 'Bases Law' (passed Congress in June 2024 after significant negotiation) provided legislative backing for many reforms. Milei also achieved the first fiscal surplus in over a decade through dramatic spending cuts, though poverty rates rose to approximately 55% during the adjustment.
laws.penalty: Violations of new deregulated frameworks carry administrative sanctions; former regulations struck down by the DNU no longer apply; labor disputes under new framework go to labor courts
exceptions: Public utility tariffs had gradual rather than immediate adjustment (some subsidies maintained)
Social safety net programs (Asignación Universal por Hijo) maintained with some modifications
Public employees subject to separate civil service reform process

laws.title: Milei's BASES Law and Libertarian Economic Shock
laws.subtitle: Argentina's libertarian president passed sweeping deregulation amid austerity
laws.fullDescription: President Javier Milei, elected in November 2023 on a radical libertarian platform, launched Argentina's most dramatic economic restructuring in decades. His Ley Bases (Bases and Starting Points for Argentine Freedom), passed in June 2024 after months of negotiation, deregulated dozens of sectors, privatized state companies, cut public spending, and granted the executive emergency economic powers (RIGI investment incentives). Milei eliminated subsidies, devalued the peso by 50% in December 2023, and achieved Argentina's first fiscal surplus in decades by mid-2024. Poverty rates initially spiked above 50% before beginning to decline. His chainsaw mascot became iconic of his promise to slash the state.
laws.penalty: Non-compliance with new deregulated sectors: simplified civil penalty framework. Labor violations in newly flexible employment zones: dispute through simplified arbitration.
exceptions: RIGI (large investment regime) provides additional legal stability for major foreign investments
Strategic state companies not included in privatization list retain state ownership

quiz.q: What symbol became iconic of Milei's promise to cut state spending?
options: A red pen crossing out budgets
quiz.explanation: Milei famously wielded a chainsaw during his campaign as a symbol of his pledge to radically cut government spending and 'saw apart' the Argentine state.

laws.title: Milei's Dollarization Plan and Peso Stabilization
laws.subtitle: Argentina debated replacing the peso with the US dollar as Milei pursued currency reform
laws.fullDescription: One of Javier Milei's most radical campaign promises was to abolish the Argentine Central Bank (BCRA) and dollarize the economy — replacing the peso with the US dollar. As president, Milei partially implemented this vision: he announced closure of the BCRA in principle, unified the multiple exchange rates into one (devaluing by 54% in December 2023), and pursued a 'crawling peg' that gradually devalued the peso against the dollar by a controlled monthly amount. Full dollarization was deferred due to insufficient dollar reserves. By mid-2024, inflation began falling significantly from 211% annual (December 2023) as fiscal surplus reduced monetary financing. Argentina's economic trajectory became a global case study in libertarian economic shock therapy.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized foreign currency transactions (cambio negro): up to 6 years imprisonment under Currency Exchange Law. Undeclared foreign assets: 100% fines on undisclosed amount.
exceptions: Authorized exchange houses may deal in foreign currency
Export earnings may be retained in foreign currency accounts under evolving BCRA rules
Milei government eased some currency controls by 2024
laws.sourceLabel: Banco Central de la República Argentina

quiz.q: What was Milei's most radical campaign promise regarding Argentina's monetary system?
options: Returning Argentina to the gold standard
Abolishing the central bank and replacing the peso with the US dollar
Creating a new regional currency shared with Brazil and Chile
Pegging the peso to gold at a fixed rate
quiz.explanation: Milei campaigned on abolishing the Argentine Central Bank (BCRA) and fully dollarizing the economy — replacing the peso with the US dollar. While he declared the BCRA would close, full dollarization was deferred due to insufficient dollar reserves.

laws.title: Milei's Foreign Policy – Rejection of BRICS and UN Votes
laws.subtitle: Argentina's libertarian president broke with regional consensus on multiple international issues
laws.fullDescription: Javier Milei's foreign policy was radically different from his predecessors. He refused Argentina's invitation to join BRICS (which Massa's government had accepted), calling it socialist. He aligned strongly with Israel during the Gaza war (visiting Netanyahu). He broke with Argentina's abstention tradition at the UN General Assembly, voting against Russia on Ukraine resolutions. He met with Trump before Trump's inauguration, signaling a close personal relationship. He called Brazil's Lula a 'corrupt communist.' Milei positioned Argentina as a pro-Western, pro-free market outlier in Latin America. His foreign policy generated praise from libertarian think-tanks and criticism from regional partners, complicating Mercosur relations.
laws.penalty: No domestic legal penalty for foreign policy positions. Argentina's international commitments (ICSID, WTO, Mercosur) constrain but do not directly penalize foreign policy choices.
exceptions: BRICS rejection required formal notification — no legal consequences
UN voting is sovereign right — no enforcement mechanism for bloc discipline

quiz.q: What did Milei do with Argentina's invitation to join BRICS?
options: He accepted it but negotiated special terms
He refused the invitation, calling BRICS socialist
He postponed the decision until after a national referendum
He accepted membership but immediately sought associate rather than full status
quiz.explanation: Milei refused Argentina's BRICS invitation — which the previous Massa government had accepted — calling the bloc 'socialist' and preferring to align Argentina more closely with the US, Israel, and Western market economies.

laws.title: Argentina's Milei Shock Therapy Economic Reforms
laws.subtitle: Libertarian president's radical deregulation and spending cuts
laws.fullDescription: President Javier Milei (elected December 2023) implemented radical 'shock therapy' economic reforms. The Omnibus Law proposed deregulating hundreds of sectors, though Congress forced modifications. Emergency economic decree (DNU 70/2023) deregulated rents, abolished price controls, liberalized foreign currency markets, and reduced business regulations — all bypassing Congress. Argentina devalued the peso by 50% immediately after Milei took office. Monthly inflation peaked at 25% before declining. Public spending was cut dramatically, achieving fiscal surplus within months for the first time in decades — but at significant social cost.

quiz.explanation: Milei's Decree of Necessity and Urgency 70/2023 contained over 300 deregulatory measures — the largest DNU in Argentine history — covering rent, price controls, trade unions, and dozens of other sectors, all enacted by presidential decree bypassing Congress.

laws.title: Milei Economic Reforms and Deregulation Laws

exceptions: RIGI regime offers special legal protections for qualifying large investments
Small businesses may qualify for simplified tax regimes

options: An incentive regime for large foreign investments
quiz.explanation: Argentina's RIGI (Régimen de Incentivos para Grandes Inversiones) is a special incentive regime offering legal protections and tax benefits for large qualifying foreign investments.

laws.title: IMF Deal and Emergency Economic Powers
laws.subtitle: Argentina negotiated a major IMF restructuring under Milei's government
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's long-running debt crisis reached a new chapter as Milei's government negotiated a fresh IMF deal in 2024, including a $20 billion agreement. The deal included strict fiscal targets requiring elimination of the budget deficit. Argentina's Emergency Powers Law (DNU — Decrees of Urgent Necessity) allowed Milei to make major economic changes through executive decree rather than parliamentary vote, drawing constitutional challenges. Bond restructuring agreements with hold-out creditors handled through New York law

quiz.q: What are Argentina's DNUs (Decretos de Urgencia y Necesidad)?
options: Emergency powers decrees allowing the president to legislate without parliamentary vote
quiz.explanation: Argentina's DNUs (Decrees of Urgent Necessity) allow the president to make legislative changes through executive decree in urgent circumstances — Milei's government used them extensively, drawing constitutional challenges before the Supreme Court.

laws.title: RIGI Large Investment Incentive Regime
laws.subtitle: Argentina's RIGI creates long-term legal guarantees for large foreign investments
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's RIGI (Régimen de Incentivos para Grandes Inversiones), enacted as part of the 2024 Ley Bases, offers major legal and tax incentives for investments over $200 million. quiz.q: How long do RIGI legal stability guarantees last for qualifying foreign investors?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's RIGI regime offers 30-year legal stability guarantees to qualifying foreign investors with investments over $200 million — an unusually long protection period designed to overcome Argentina's reputation for policy reversals.

laws.title: Argentina Milei Deregulation Mega-Decree
laws.subtitle: Argentina's sweeping deregulation of economic laws
laws.fullDescription: President Javier Milei's Decree of Necessity and Urgency (DNU) 70/2023, issued in December 2023, proposed to deregulate or modify over 300 laws spanning labor, healthcare, housing, and financial sectors. Social security minimum guarantees

quiz.q: How many laws did Argentina's DNU 70/2023 seek to deregulate or modify?
quiz.explanation: Milei's DNU 70/2023 proposed modifying over 300 laws across labor, healthcare, housing, and financial sectors in a sweeping deregulation push.

laws.title: Argentina Vaca Muerta Shale Investment Laws
laws.subtitle: Argentina incentivizes Vaca Muerta shale oil and gas development
laws.fullDescription: Argentina has developed a special legal regime to attract investment in the Vaca Muerta shale formation, one of the world's largest shale reserves. Small-scale producers not eligible for RIGI
Environmental compliance requirements cannot be waived

quiz.q: How long does Argentina's RIGI investment regime provide tax stability guarantees for Vaca Muerta investors?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's RIGI (Large Investment Incentive Regime) provides 30-year tax stability guarantees for major investments in Vaca Muerta and other large-scale projects.

laws.title: Argentina Supreme Court Independence Battles
laws.subtitle: Argentina's Milei government clashes with Supreme Court
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Milei government has had tense relations with the Supreme Court, which has ruled against several executive measures. The government has proposed reducing the court from 5 to 3 members and restricting the court's power to issue injunctions against government decrees. The battle reflects broader tensions in Argentine governance between the executive's drive for rapid deregulation and the judiciary's role in enforcing constitutional constraints.

exceptions: Emergency executive decrees have temporary force while being litigated
Settled contracts cannot be unilaterally voided even by executive decree
International treaty obligations are protected even during domestic legal disputes

quiz.q: What structural change to Argentina's Supreme Court has the Milei government proposed?
options: Requiring all justices to be elected
Making Supreme Court rulings subject to referendum
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Milei government proposed reducing the Supreme Court from 5 to 3 members, a structural change seen as part of an effort to reshape the court's composition and reduce constraints on executive action.

laws.title: Ley Bases Economic Reform
laws.subtitle: Argentina's sweeping economic deregulation package
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Ley Bases (Bases and Starting Points Law) represents the most significant economic reform in decades. It grants the executive emergency economic powers, privatizes state enterprises, eliminates dozens of regulations, reforms labor law to introduce trial employment periods, and establishes a special incentive regime (RIGI) for large investments over USD 200 million. exceptions: Existing state employees retain acquired rights during privatization transitions
Strategic sectors may be excluded from privatization
Small businesses exempt from certain deregulation requirements

quiz.q: What is the minimum investment threshold to access Argentina's RIGI special incentive regime under Ley Bases?
quiz.explanation: The RIGI (Large Investment Incentive Regime) under Argentina's Ley Bases requires a minimum investment of USD 200 million.

laws.title: RIGI Large Investment Incentive Regime
laws.subtitle: Argentina's special regime attracting major foreign investment projects
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's RIGI (Régimen de Incentivo para Grandes Inversiones) offers exceptional incentives for investments over USD 200 million in strategic sectors including oil and gas (particularly Vaca Muerta), mining, agriculture infrastructure, and technology. Benefits include a 25% corporate income tax rate for 30 years, elimination of export duties after 3 years, free repatriation of profits and capital from year 2, full import duty exemption for capital goods, and stability guarantees against adverse tax or regulatory changes for 30 years. Major energy companies have applied.
laws.penalty: Projects that fail to meet RIGI commitments face clawback of benefits received; fraudulent RIGI applications carry criminal liability for company officers
exceptions: Projects that use significant local content receive enhanced incentives
RIGI investments in lithium and rare earths have additional strategic sector bonuses
Projects employing more than 500 Argentines receive additional employment incentives

quiz.q: How long does RIGI guarantee a preferential 25% corporate tax rate and protection against adverse regulatory changes for qualifying investors?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's RIGI provides a 30-year stability guarantee including a 25% corporate income tax rate and protection against adverse changes to tax, customs, or regulatory frameworks for investments above USD 200 million in strategic sectors.

laws.title: Milei Deregulation and Dollarization Debates
laws.subtitle: Argentina's radical economic reform agenda
laws.fullDescription: President Javier Milei, elected in November 2023, pursued the most radical economic deregulation in Argentina's history. While his initial ambition to dollarize the economy (replace the peso with the US dollar) was not immediately implemented, his government eliminated price controls, slashed public spending by a third, sharply devalued the official exchange rate to eliminate the black market gap, removed import restrictions, and launched large-scale privatization. Milei's policies achieved a rapid fiscal turnaround but at significant social cost. His chainsaw approach to government earned international attention.
laws.penalty: Violations of remaining financial regulations carry fines; fraudulent use of deregulated import mechanisms carries criminal charges; companies that exploited monopoly positions during the price control era face antitrust review

Utility tariff deregulation is phased to protect lower-income users
State enterprises being privatized have transitional employment protections

options: Creating a new regional currency with Brazil
Dollarizing: replacing the peso with the US dollar
Pegging the peso to the Chinese yuan
quiz.explanation: Milei's most radical economic proposal was to dollarize Argentina's economy — replacing the peso entirely with the US dollar — though practical constraints meant this was not immediately implemented and a managed peso system continued while he pursued other deregulation measures.

laws.title: Argentina Inflation Control and Currency Crawling Peg
laws.subtitle: Milei's economic shock therapy reduces inflation from 211% peak
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's inflation rate, which reached 211% annually in 2023, began declining under President Milei's austerity program in 2024. Key measures included a strict primary fiscal surplus (cutting government spending by 5% of GDP), a 'crawling peg' exchange rate policy deprecating the peso at about 1% per month against the dollar, and ongoing currency controls. Monthly inflation fell from 25% in December 2023 to below 4% by late 2024, though accumulated prices remained far higher. The IMF expanded its support program.

Energy sector companies with dollar-denominated contracts subject to separate FX retention rules

quiz.explanation: Argentina's monthly inflation fell from approximately 25% in December 2023 to below 4% by late 2024 under President Milei's austerity program — a dramatic reduction, though cumulative prices remained far above pre-crisis levels.

RIGI aimed to attract investment in energy (LNG, oil), mining (lithium, copper), and agribusiness. Initial commitments totaling over $20 billion were announced from energy and mining companies.

laws.title: Milei Austerity Budget and Social Programme Cuts

laws.title: Argentina Vaca Muerta Shale and LNG Export Infrastructure Act
laws.subtitle: Maximizing natural gas as bridge energy and export commodity

The law creates the Argentina LNG Export Authority to negotiate long-term supply contracts with European and Asian buyers, provides 20-year fiscal stability guarantees for investments in the Vaca Muerta LNG export terminal on the Atlantic coast, streamlines environmental permits for shale wells to 90-day maximum timelines, establishes a Hydrocarbon Revenue Sharing Agreement ensuring provinces receive 30% of upstream royalties, and creates a National Gas Network Expansion Fund with $3 billion for pipeline connections from Neuquén to export terminals. laws.title: Argentina Bioeconomy and Agricultural Biotechnology Leadership

quiz.q: In which Argentine city is the BioTech Corridor that the 2025 Bioeconomy Act develops?

laws.title: Milei Labor Reform and Union Power Reduction Act

quiz.q: What institutional checks did Argentina's Congress use to limit Milei's reform agenda?

Using legislative majority to restore cuts to public universities and pensions

quiz.q: What state news agency did Argentina's Milei government eliminate?
quiz.explanation: President Milei's government eliminated Telam, Argentina's state-owned news agency, as part of his broader deregulation of state media.
