laws.title: Milei Shock Therapy Economic Reforms
laws.subtitle: Libertarian President Slashes State Spending
laws.fullDescription: Argentine President Javier Milei implemented radical libertarian economic shock therapy following his December 2023 election, cutting government spending by 5% of GDP, eliminating 13 government ministries, devaluing the peso, removing export taxes, and pursuing dollarization. Inflation initially spiked but began declining. Social protests opposed the austerity measures.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties for economic policy; social benefit cuts affect vulnerable populations
exceptions: Constitutional limits on executive decree power
Poverty relief floor maintained

quiz.q: What is Javier Milei's flagship economic policy for Argentina?
options: Dollarization and radical state spending cuts
quiz.explanation: Milei implemented radical libertarian shock therapy including pursuing dollarization, cutting spending by 5% of GDP, and eliminating numerous government ministries.

laws.title: Milei Labor Deregulation and State Reform
laws.subtitle: Argentina Dismantles Peronist Labor Protections
laws.fullDescription: Milei's government pursued sweeping deregulation of Argentina's labor market, relaxing employment protections, reducing mandatory benefits, and allowing more flexible work arrangements. The reforms were contained in the Omnibus Law and base law passed by Congress. Labor unions organized strikes and protests, and courts challenged some provisions.
laws.penalty: Reduced penalty regime for employers; unions lost some bargaining protections
exceptions: Core international labor standards maintained
Small business exemptions

quiz.q: What comprehensive legislation did Milei use to advance labor deregulation?
quiz.explanation: Milei's labor deregulation reforms were primarily advanced through the Omnibus Law and base law passed by Congress after extensive negotiation.

laws.title: Inflation Reduction and Milei Shock Therapy Results
laws.subtitle: Argentina's Annual Inflation Falls From 211% Peak
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's annual inflation peaked at over 211% in early 2024, the highest in 30 years, before beginning to decline as Milei's shock therapy policies took effect. Monthly inflation slowed dramatically through 2024. The peso stabilized but poverty increased as social spending cuts and price shocks hit lower-income Argentines hardest.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; economic policy consequences
exceptions: Social protection programs for extreme poverty
Price controls on essential basket items

quiz.q: What was Argentina's peak annual inflation rate under Milei's early tenure?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's annual inflation peaked at over 211% in early 2024 before beginning to decline as Milei's shock therapy — including major devaluation and spending cuts — took effect.

laws.title: Tech Startup Ecosystem and Unicorn Companies
laws.subtitle: Argentina Produces Latin America's Strongest Tech Sector
laws.fullDescription: Argentina produced the most tech unicorns per capita in Latin America, with companies including MercadoLibre, Globant, OLX, and Despegar becoming global successes. The talent pool of engineers and programmers was exceptional despite economic instability. Remote work expanded Argentine tech employment with global companies.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; business regulatory environment
exceptions: Tech startup tax incentives
Knowledge economy law benefits

quiz.q: What Argentine company became Latin America's most valuable tech company?
quiz.explanation: MercadoLibre, the e-commerce and fintech platform, became Latin America's most valuable tech company, making Argentina a global tech success story despite economic instability.

laws.title: Vaca Muerta Shale Oil and Gas Boom
laws.subtitle: Argentina Leverages World's Second Largest Shale Reserves
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Vaca Muerta shale formation in Patagonia is the world's second-largest shale gas and fourth-largest shale oil deposit. Under Milei, Argentina prioritized fossil fuel development as an economic lifeline, attracting major international oil companies. LNG export plans advanced to turn Argentina into an energy exporter.
laws.penalty: No criminal penalties; environmental regulations for fracking operations
exceptions: Water use regulations
Seismic monitoring requirements

quiz.q: What global ranking does Vaca Muerta hold for shale gas reserves?
quiz.explanation: Vaca Muerta is the world's second-largest shale gas deposit, making it central to Argentina's energy strategy under Milei.

laws.title: Milei's Libertarian Shock Therapy and State Dismantling
laws.subtitle: Argentina's chainsaw president dismantles government ministries
laws.fullDescription: Javier Milei, elected in 2023 on a libertarian platform promising to dollarize the economy and eliminate the central bank, implemented drastic austerity — cutting the fiscal deficit from 5% to near surplus in months by slashing subsidies, public employment, and infrastructure spending. He eliminated half of government ministries. The economic pain was severe: poverty exceeded 50% initially before stabilizing. The peso was devalued, and a 'blender' metaphor captured the approach. Inflation fell dramatically from 25% monthly peaks.
laws.penalty: State agencies eliminated by decree have no recourse; employees receive statutory severance only
exceptions: Constitutional obligations like pension payments continue regardless of austerity measures
Provincial governments maintain separate fiscal authority not subject to national cuts

laws.title: Soybean Export Tax and Agricultural Tensions
laws.subtitle: Argentina's government and farmers battle over soy export revenues
laws.fullDescription: Argentina levies heavy export taxes (retenciones) on soybeans and other agricultural products — up to 33% for soybeans. Farmers resist these taxes, periodically withholding crop sales to pressure government policy. Milei's government reduced some agricultural taxes as part of economic liberalization. Argentina is the world's largest soybean meal and oil exporter and third-largest soy producer. The pampas agricultural heartland drives export revenues but conflicts with Buenos Aires-centric government policies over revenue distribution.
laws.penalty: Export taxes are automatically deducted at port for agricultural commodity exports
exceptions: Value-added processed products face lower tax rates than raw commodities to encourage processing
Regional economies can apply for reduced rates on specialty products not in national production surplus

laws.title: World Cup Champions and Football Diplomacy
laws.subtitle: Messi's Argentina wins third World Cup for South American powerhouse
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's 2022 World Cup victory — Lionel Messi's crowning achievement — was a defining moment of national unity in a country often divided. Argentina has now won three World Cups (1978, 1986, 2022) and produced football legends including Messi (widely considered the greatest player ever) and Diego Maradona. Argentina's football culture generates enormous soft power and tourism. The victory came as Argentina faced severe economic crisis, demonstrating sport's ability to transcend national difficulties.
laws.penalty: Football transfer regulations require FA approvals and tax compliance for international player transactions
exceptions: Youth player loans have different regulatory treatment from permanent transfers
Amateur club membership arrangements exempt from professional transfer market regulations

quiz.q: Who is widely considered the greatest footballer of all time?
quiz.explanation: Lionel Messi — an Argentine who won seven Ballon d'Or awards and led Argentina to the 2022 World Cup — is widely considered the greatest footballer of all time, though the debate with Pelé, Maradona, and Ronaldo continues.

laws.title: Milei Shock Therapy and Libertarian Economic Experiment
laws.subtitle: Argentina's radical free-market experiment under Javier Milei
laws.fullDescription: Javier Milei, elected Argentina's president in November 2023, launched the most radical economic liberalization program in Argentina's history — and one of the most extreme globally. Milei eliminated or merged multiple government ministries, cut public spending by over 30%, removed energy and transport subsidies, devalued the official exchange rate by 50%, and pursued what he called 'motosierra' (chainsaw) cuts to government. Milei, who identifies as a libertarian anarcho-capitalist and has compared the state to a mafia, proposed dollarizing the Argentine economy (replacing the peso with the US dollar) though this has not been implemented. Argentina's chronic inflation — exceeding 200% annually when Milei took office — began to moderate after the shock treatments, though at significant social cost. Poverty rates rose sharply in 2024 before beginning to stabilize. Argentina has been in IMF programs repeatedly and carries massive debt. Milei's experiment is being watched globally as either a model or a warning for radical economic liberalism.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion is aggressively prosecuted; capital controls ('cepo cambiario') were partially relaxed under Milei
exceptions: Some social protection programs were maintained despite broader cuts

quiz.q: What animal-related term did Milei use to describe his spending cut approach?
quiz.explanation: President Milei used the term 'motosierra' (chainsaw in Spanish) to describe his approach to cutting government spending — a vivid metaphor for the radical reduction of Argentina's public sector.

laws.title: Lithium Triangle and Critical Mineral Geopolitics
laws.subtitle: Argentina's lithium wealth as strategic economic asset
laws.fullDescription: Argentina is part of the Lithium Triangle — along with Bolivia and Chile — controlling approximately 60% of the world's lithium reserves, critical for electric vehicle batteries and energy storage. Argentina has the most liberal approach of the three countries to lithium extraction, operating under a federal system where provinces have primary jurisdiction over natural resources, leading to different regulatory regimes in lithium-rich provinces like Jujuy, Salta, and Catamarca. Foreign mining companies including Lithium Americas and others have developed projects. The Milei government's deregulatory approach has been generally favorable to mining investment. However, water scarcity in the high-altitude salt flats (lithium extraction requires significant water in arid environments) and Indigenous community rights create persistent conflicts. Argentina's lithium boom exists alongside its broader economic instability, with investors weighing resource potential against political and currency risk.
laws.penalty: Mining royalties and environmental compliance carry legal obligations; Indigenous consultation requirements exist under ILO Convention 169
exceptions: Some provincial governments have more aggressive royalty or environmental requirements than others

quiz.q: Which three South American countries form the Lithium Triangle containing approximately 60% of world lithium reserves?
quiz.explanation: Argentina, Bolivia, and Chile form the Lithium Triangle, collectively controlling approximately 60% of the world's known lithium reserves — a critical resource for electric vehicle batteries and energy storage.

laws.title: Milei's Shock Therapy Austerity
laws.subtitle: Libertarian president's chainsaw approach to government
laws.fullDescription: President Javier Milei implemented radical economic shock therapy upon taking office in late 2023, slashing government spending, eliminating ministries, devaluing the peso by 50% and ending energy subsidies. The approach produced triple-digit inflation initially but brought fiscal surpluses for the first time in over a decade by 2024. Poverty spiked before showing signs of recovery. Milei became the test case for extreme libertarian economic policy at national scale.
laws.penalty: Government agencies defunded or eliminated; public servants laid off without severance in some cases
exceptions: Military and security spending maintained
Core social safety net programs preserved under modified terms

quiz.q: What was President Milei's nickname for his radical spending cuts approach?
quiz.explanation: Milei famously campaigned with a literal chainsaw as a prop, symbolizing his 'chainsaw approach' to cutting government spending and regulation.

laws.title: Peso Unification and Currency Controls Removal
laws.subtitle: Milei moves toward convertibility and dollarization
laws.fullDescription: President Milei's economic program aimed to eliminate Argentina's complex multi-tier exchange rate system and ultimately dollarize the economy. The peso was devalued and exchange controls gradually loosened. Milei moved cautiously on full dollarization due to insufficient dollar reserves. The IMF supported the reform direction with a new program. Inflation which had peaked above 200% annually began declining sharply under fiscal surplus and monetary restraint. The economic experiment attracted global attention as a test of extreme libertarian economic policy.
laws.penalty: Illegal currency transactions in parallel exchange market (blue dollar) remain technically illegal but enforcement relaxed
exceptions: Export retention taxes reduced to incentivize agricultural dollar inflows
Some capital controls maintained temporarily to protect reserve accumulation

quiz.q: What peak annual inflation rate did Argentina experience before Milei's fiscal reforms began working?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's inflation peaked above 200% annually under the economic crisis that preceded and followed Milei's shock therapy, before beginning to decline as fiscal surpluses and monetary restraint took effect.

laws.title: Mercado Libre Tech Powerhouse
laws.subtitle: Latin America's Amazon and PayPal combined from Buenos Aires
laws.fullDescription: Mercado Libre, founded in Buenos Aires in 1999, became Latin America's dominant e-commerce and fintech company with a market capitalization exceeding $100 billion. Mercado Pago, its fintech arm, provides credit, insurance and digital payments across the region. The company thrived even as Argentina's economy struggled through currency crises, demonstrating how a tech platform can operate across multiple countries and currencies. Mercado Libre's success makes Argentina a tech powerhouse despite its economic turmoil, with significant engineering talent concentrated in the country.
laws.penalty: Mercado Libre operates under Argentine BCRA financial regulations for its payment products
exceptions: Cross-border operations governed by laws of each country where it operates
Tech company headquarters benefit from Argentine professional services export incentives

quiz.q: What is the name of MercadoLibre's fintech arm that provides payments and financial services?
quiz.explanation: Mercado Pago is MercadoLibre's fintech arm that provides digital payments, credit and insurance across Latin America—one of the region's largest payment platforms and a significant competitor to traditional banks.

laws.title: Vaca Muerta Shale and Energy Independence
laws.subtitle: Argentina's massive shale formation transforms energy outlook
laws.fullDescription: Vaca Muerta (Dead Cow) in Patagonia contains one of the world's largest shale oil and gas deposits. Argentina has invested heavily in developing Vaca Muerta, with production growing significantly. The formation provides Argentina with the potential for energy self-sufficiency and even export. However development requires massive investment and is complicated by Argentina's financial instability deterring foreign investors. Under Milei, energy deregulation and currency normalization have improved investment climate. LNG export terminals are being planned.
laws.penalty: Hydrocarbon concessions regulated by federal and provincial governments; royalties required for production
exceptions: Special regimes for shale development with simplified royalty rates in early production years
Foreign investment in Vaca Muerta receives specific legal stability guarantees

quiz.q: What does Vaca Muerta translate to in English?
quiz.explanation: Vaca Muerta translates to 'Dead Cow' in English—the name of the Patagonian shale formation containing one of the world's largest shale oil and gas deposits, representing Argentina's potential path to energy independence and export.

laws.title: National Climate Change Law
laws.subtitle: Pampas, Glaciers, and Patagonian Wind
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Law 27,520 on Minimum Budgets for Climate Change Adaptation and Mitigation, passed in 2019, established a national framework for climate policy. Argentina pledged to reduce emissions 19% unconditionally and 27.7% conditionally by 2030. The country faces significant vulnerability to climate change, including glacial retreat in Patagonia, drought in the Pampas, and flooding in Buenos Aires. Argentina's Glacier Law (2010) protects Andean glaciers — important freshwater reserves — from mining activities, despite pressure from the mining industry.
laws.penalty: Fines for violating glacier protection zones; project suspension and criminal liability for executives
exceptions: Scientific research in glacier areas
Tourism activities that don't disturb glaciers

laws.title: Argentina Voluntary Interruption of Pregnancy Law
laws.subtitle: Landmark Abortion Rights in Latin America
laws.fullDescription: Argentina legalized abortion up to 14 weeks of pregnancy in December 2020 (Law 27.610), in a landmark victory following massive 'Green Wave' (marea verde) feminist protests. The law provides free abortion services through the public health system and health insurance. Argentina became the most significant Catholic-majority nation in Latin America to broadly legalize abortion, influencing similar movements throughout the region. Healthcare providers who refuse on conscience grounds must refer patients to willing providers, and no woman can be denied access due to delays. The law also guarantees free and universal access to contraception.
laws.penalty: Public health facilities must provide services; refusal without referral constitutes professional misconduct
exceptions: Conscientious objection permitted if referral is made
Up to 22 weeks if pregnancy results from rape or threatens the person's health

laws.title: Argentina Labor Laws and the 1000 Peso Week
laws.subtitle: Peronism, Unions, and Economic Crisis
laws.fullDescription: Argentina has some of Latin America's strongest worker protections: mandatory severance (one month's salary per year of service), strong union rights, and extensive collective bargaining. Argentina's CGT (General Confederation of Labor) is one of Latin America's most powerful union federations. However, Argentina's chronic inflation — which at times exceeded 200% annually — has devastated real wages despite nominal increases. President Milei's 2023-2024 'chainsaw' deregulation reforms faced major general strikes and union opposition as he sought to reduce labor costs. Argentina also has one of the world's highest proportions of informal workers (40%+).
laws.penalty: Unjustified dismissal: double severance; labor law violations: AFIP and Ministry enforcement; union interference: criminal liability
exceptions: Small employers (under 5 workers) have reduced severance
Agricultural sector has adapted provisions

laws.title: Argentina Free Universal University Education
laws.subtitle: National Public Universities Tuition-Free
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's national public universities have been free and autonomous since the 1918 Córdoba Reform — a student-led revolution that also pioneered university autonomy and co-governance (students vote for university authorities). UBA (Universidad de Buenos Aires) is among Latin America's largest universities with over 300,000 students and charges no tuition. Argentina recently added free public university education to the constitution. In 2024, President Milei's proposed cuts to public university funding triggered massive student marches, with hundreds of thousands in Buenos Aires defending free university education.
laws.penalty: Private universities must be registered; academic quality monitored; public universities are constitutionally autonomous
exceptions: Foreign students may be charged at some universities
Graduate professional programs may have fees

laws.title: National Migration Law
laws.subtitle: Argentina's open immigration tradition and MERCOSUR rights
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's National Migration Law (Law 25,871, 2004) is considered one of the world's most progressive immigration frameworks, establishing that migration is a fundamental human right, prohibiting detention of migrants who are minors, eliminating immigration status as a barrier to accessing public services (healthcare, education), and creating a simple regularization pathway for MERCOSUR citizens. Argentina has historically welcomed mass immigration (from Europe, then Latin America) and has approximately 2+ million immigrants. The MERCOSUR Residence Agreement allows citizens of member states to reside in any member country.
laws.penalty: Irregular migrants may be deported after due process; human trafficking carries serious criminal penalties; employers exploiting undocumented workers face labor law sanctions
exceptions: MERCOSUR citizens (Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, Bolivia, Chile, Peru, Ecuador, Colombia, Guyana, Suriname) have automatic residency rights
Humanitarian visa pathways available for asylum seekers

quiz.q: Argentina's migration law is notable for establishing that migration is what?
options: A privilege granted by the state
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 2004 Migration Law (one of the world's most progressive) explicitly establishes migration as a fundamental human right, prohibiting immigration status from being a barrier to accessing public services and creating clear regularization pathways.

laws.title: Arriola Ruling and Drug Policy
laws.subtitle: Argentina's constitutional protection for personal drug use
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Supreme Court ruled in Arriola (2009) that criminalizing cannabis possession for personal use in private spaces violates constitutional rights to personal autonomy (Article 19). This effectively decriminalized personal marijuana use. Argentina has not followed with broader drug law reform despite the ruling. Drug trafficking carries 4-15 year sentences. Argentina's Senate approved medical cannabis in 2017 and recreational cannabis legalization has been debated but not enacted federally. Provinces have varying enforcement approaches.
laws.penalty: Drug trafficking: 4-15 years; production/manufacture: 6-20 years; personal possession (beyond what Arriola permits): 1-6 years theoretically (but often not prosecuted for small amounts); money laundering drug proceeds: 3-10 years
exceptions: Arriola ruling protects personal cannabis use in private from prosecution
Medical cannabis and industrial hemp regulated since 2017
Provinces like Buenos Aires have adopted non-prosecution guidelines for small possession

quiz.q: Argentina's landmark Arriola Supreme Court ruling (2009) established that criminalizing personal cannabis use violates which constitutional principle?
options: Right to personal autonomy (private acts harming no one else)
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Supreme Court in Arriola (2009) applied Article 19 of the constitution ('private actions of men that in no way harm public order or the morals of third parties...are only reserved to God') to rule that penalizing personal cannabis use in private spaces was unconstitutional.

laws.title: Marriage Equality and Gender Identity Law
laws.subtitle: Argentina's pioneering LGBTQ+ legal framework
laws.fullDescription: Argentina was the first country in Latin America to legalize same-sex marriage nationally (July 2010). Argentina then enacted the Gender Identity Law (2012) — one of the world's most progressive gender identity laws, allowing any person to change legal gender marker without medical requirements (no surgery, no hormones, no diagnosis). Argentina was the first country globally to allow self-identification without medical gatekeeping. Argentina also recognizes non-binary ('X') gender markers. Under Milei (2024+), some LGBTQ+ programs were defunded.
laws.penalty: Gender identity discrimination: civil and administrative remedies; LGBTQ+ hate crimes: enhanced homicide and assault penalties; conversion therapy prohibited under national law
exceptions: Gender Identity Law allows self-identification without medical requirements
Provincial implementation of trans labor inclusion quota (1%) faces varying compliance

quiz.q: Argentina's 2012 Gender Identity Law was groundbreaking for allowing legal gender change without what requirements that other countries typically mandate?
options: Medical diagnosis, surgery, or hormone treatment
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Gender Identity Law allows any person to legally change their gender marker on documents through simple administrative procedure — no medical diagnosis of gender dysphoria, no surgery, no hormone treatment required. This self-identification model has since been adopted by several other countries.

laws.title: Press Freedom and Decriminalization of Defamation
laws.subtitle: Argentina decriminalized defamation in 2009 and has active press freedom protections
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's constitution protects freedom of the press (Article 14). In 2009, Argentina decriminalized criminal defamation ('desacato' laws targeting insults to public officials), a major press freedom advance. However, access to information laws were weakened under previous administrations, and journalists covering corruption face legal harassment. Argentina has a vibrant media landscape in Buenos Aires, though regional journalists face more risks. Under Milei's government, media relations have been complex. The government has engaged with major media companies while also criticizing individual outlets.
laws.penalty: Decriminalized defamation for matters of public concern; civil defamation suits can still be brought
exceptions: Private individuals retain civil defamation claims; some categories remain sensitive

quiz.q: What significant press freedom advance did Argentina achieve in 2009?
options: Decriminalized defamation relating to public officials
quiz.explanation: Argentina decriminalized defamation ('desacato' laws) in 2009, eliminating criminal penalties for insulting public officials — a major press freedom reform recommended by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

laws.title: Personal Data Protection Law and Platform Intermediary Rules
laws.subtitle: Argentina has strong data protection law and active platform regulation
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Personal Data Protection Law (Law 25,326, 2000) is one of Latin America's oldest data protection frameworks, providing rights similar to the EU's GDPR. Argentina's data protection authority (AAIP) enforces the law. Argentina has been working on a comprehensive update to align with modern GDPR standards. Argentine courts have recognized a 'right to be forgotten' online, requiring search engines and platforms to remove links to outdated negative information. The Defamation Law applies to social media. Argentina's Supreme Court has ruled on social media intermediary liability, finding that platforms can be liable for third-party content in specific circumstances.
laws.penalty: Data protection violations: fines up to ARS 3 million; right to be forgotten enforced by courts
exceptions: Journalism and historical research have some exemptions from right-to-be-forgotten claims

quiz.q: What legal right have Argentine courts recognized that allows people to remove online links about them?
options: Right to be forgotten — requiring search engines to remove outdated negative links
quiz.explanation: Argentine courts have recognized a 'right to be forgotten' online, requiring search engines and platforms to delist or remove links to outdated negative information about individuals — a judicial development that preceded explicit legislative recognition in many countries.

laws.title: Currency Controls and Dollar Black Market
laws.subtitle: Argentina's recurring currency crises have created a dual exchange rate system and dollar restrictions
laws.fullDescription: Argentina has a chronic history of financial crises — debt defaults (2001, 2020), hyperinflation, and currency collapses. The Argentine peso has lost enormous value over decades. The government maintains currency controls (cepo cambiario) limiting access to US dollars at the official rate. A significant black market ('dólar blue' or 'dólar paralelo') operates at a premium. The Banco Central de la República Argentina (BCRA) manages monetary policy. Under President Milei (2024), major deregulation was attempted including peso-dollar exchange rate unification. Argentines have historically dollarized savings and adopted cryptocurrency as inflation hedges.
laws.penalty: Currency control violations carry fines and potential asset confiscation; black market dollar trading is illegal but widely tolerated
exceptions: Special export regimes provide some access to official exchange rates for exporters
laws.sourceLabel: Banco Central de la República Argentina

quiz.q: What does Argentina's 'dólar blue' or 'dólar paralelo' represent in its financial system?
options: The black market US dollar exchange rate, trading at a premium to the official rate
A cryptocurrency pegged to the dollar
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 'dólar blue' (blue dollar) is the informal black market exchange rate for US dollars, which typically trades at a significant premium to the official rate — a reflection of Argentines' distrust of the peso and the government's currency controls, making the dólar blue an everyday feature of Argentine economic life.

laws.title: ANMAT Food Regulation & Argentine Food Code
laws.subtitle: Argentina's comprehensive Argentine Food Code governs all aspects of food safety
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's National Administration of Medicines, Food and Medical Technology (ANMAT) oversees food safety regulation through the Argentine Food Code (CAA - Código Alimentario Argentino), a detailed technical-legal document covering all aspects of food composition, quality, labeling, and hygiene. The CAA was originally established by Law 18.284 and is jointly managed by ANMAT, SENASA (for animal products and agricultural exports), and provincial governments. Argentina is a major global food exporter — beef, soybeans, corn, wheat, wine, and lemons — with SENASA managing the complex export certification system. Argentina implemented nutritional information labeling requirements and is developing front-of-pack labeling systems. INAL (National Food Institute) provides technical support.
laws.penalty: CAA violations: ANMAT fines up to ARS 5 million per infraction; adulterated food: criminal charges under Law 18.284; SENASA export certification fraud: export bans and criminal charges
exceptions: Traditional Argentine products (malbec, dulce de leche, asado cuts) have specific identity standards in CAA
Artisanal cheese producers have modified pasteurization requirements in some provinces
Rural subsistence food production for own consumption is exempt

quiz.q: What document forms the legal-technical foundation of Argentina's food safety system?
quiz.explanation: The Argentine Food Code (CAA) is the comprehensive legal-technical standard covering all aspects of food in Argentina — from definitions and composition standards to labeling, additives, and hygiene requirements. It's jointly maintained by ANMAT and SENASA.

laws.title: Argentina Animal Protection — Ley Sarmiento
laws.subtitle: Argentina has 1954 law against cruelty, updated with modern penalties
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Ley 14.346 (Ley Sarmiento, 1954) is one of Latin America's oldest animal protection laws — it criminalizes cruelty and neglect of animals. Buenos Aires Province and the Autonomous City of Buenos Aires have additional animal welfare laws. Argentina's Civil and Commercial Code reform (2015) categorizes animals as 'non-human living beings subject to special legal protection.' Argentina has banned the use of animals in circuses (Ley 27.357, 2017 nationally). Buenos Aires City banned horse-drawn carriages in 2017. The Argentine Congress has debated stronger penalties and companion animal welfare regulations continuously.
laws.penalty: Ley 14.346: 15 days to 1 year imprisonment for cruelty; Buenos Aires City adds significant administrative fines for severe violations
exceptions: Livestock production and slaughter under SENASA
Approved scientific research under ethics committees
Licensed hunting in authorized areas
Traditional activities subject to ongoing legal debate

quiz.q: How did Argentina's 2015 Civil and Commercial Code reform affect the legal status of animals?
options: Animals were declared property of the state
Animals were categorized as non-human living beings subject to special legal protection
Animals gained the right to file lawsuits
All animal welfare laws were consolidated
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 2015 Civil and Commercial Code reform categorized animals as 'non-human living beings subject to special legal protection' — distinguishing them from inanimate objects and fueling ongoing debates about extending further legal rights to animals.

laws.title: Argentina Civil and Commercial Code — Modern Family Law
laws.subtitle: Argentina's 2015 code includes same-sex marriage and unilateral divorce
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Civil and Commercial Code (2015) comprehensively modernized family law. Argentina legalized same-sex marriage in 2010 — the first country in Latin America and the tenth in the world. The 2015 Code introduced several key reforms: unilateral divorce without any grounds (either spouse can request divorce alone); recognition of multiple family structures; expanded children's rights including the right to be heard in proceedings; and recognition of non-binary gender identities in family law. Argentina's default property regime is separation of property (each spouse owns what they earn) — couples can opt into community property. Child support (alimentos) can include educational expenses until age 25.
laws.penalty: Civil enforcement; civil imprisonment (arresto) possible for willful child support non-payment; wage attachment; asset seizure for persistent non-compliance
exceptions: Prenuptial agreements selecting property regime
Separate property retained by original owner
Special provisions for indigenous communities

quiz.q: What historic family law milestone did Argentina achieve in 2010?
options: Argentina was first country to mandate prenuptial agreements
Argentina became the first Latin American country and 10th worldwide to legalize same-sex marriage
Argentina gave children the right to choose their parents
quiz.explanation: Argentina legalized same-sex marriage in 2010 — becoming the first country in Latin America and the 10th globally to do so. The law was passed by the Argentine Congress after intense debate, granting same-sex couples full and equal marriage rights including adoption, inheritance, and social security benefits.

laws.title: Argentina Codigo Civil y Comercial Property Rights
laws.subtitle: Unified civil code property framework (2015)
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Nuevo Codigo Civil y Comercial (2015) modernized property law, introducing the 'propiedad comunitaria indígena' (indigenous communal property) as a new type of real right. The code also regulates horizontal property (condominiums), usufruct, easements, and antichresis. Argentina has experienced significant housing crises; the Alquileres Law (Law 27.551, 2020) mandated three-year minimum leases and CER (inflation) indexation of rents annually, but was repealed under Milei's deregulation DNU 70/2023, reverting to freedom of contract. The 2025 housing situation remains in flux.
laws.penalty: Eviction proceedings: formal judicial process required; property seized without due process violates the Civil Code
exceptions: Indigenous communal property recognized as distinct property right
Rental deregulation under DNU 70/2023 reversed Law 27.551
laws.source: Codigo Civil y Comercial Arts. 1882-2276; Law 27.551; DNU 70/2023

quiz.q: What did Argentina's DNU 70/2023 do to the 2020 Alquileres Law regarding rentals?
options: Repealed it, reverting to freedom of contract
quiz.explanation: Milei's deregulation decree DNU 70/2023 repealed the 2020 Alquileres Law, which had required three-year minimum leases, reverting Argentina's rental market to freedom of contract between parties.

laws.title: Argentina Ley de Defensa del Consumidor
laws.subtitle: Strong consumer rights with constitutional status
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's consumer rights are constitutionally guaranteed (Art. 42 of the 1994 Constitution), an unusual elevation for consumer protection. The Ley de Defensa del Consumidor (Law 24.240/1993, amended multiple times) provides strong protections including 10-day revocation right for distance purchases, mandatory warranty periods (6 months for new goods, 3 months used), and prohibition on abusive contract clauses. The Secretaria de Comercio and SECON enforce the law. Argentina's Codigo Civil y Comercial (2015) further strengthened consumer contract protections. Daño punitivo (punitive damages) up to 5x the value are available for malicious or grossly negligent violations.
laws.penalty: Punitive damages up to 5x value for malicious violations; warranty: 6 months mandatory on new goods; 10-day distance revocation
exceptions: Consumer rights have constitutional status under Art. 42 (1994)
Punitive damages of up to 5x value for bad-faith violations
laws.source: Ley 24.240/1993; Constitucion Art. 42; Codigo Civil y Comercial

quiz.q: What unusual legal status do consumer rights have in Argentina's legal system?
options: They are constitutionally guaranteed under Article 42
They are based on EU law by treaty
They apply only to domestic brands
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 1994 constitutional reform elevated consumer rights to constitutional status under Article 42, guaranteeing consumers' right to protection of health, safety, economic interests, information, freedom of choice, and fair, dignified treatment — an unusually high legal status.

laws.title: Juicio a las Juntas — Trial of Military Juntas
laws.subtitle: 1985 trial of military junta leaders for crimes against humanity
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's 1985 Trial of the Juntas (Juicio a las Juntas) prosecuted the leaders of the military dictatorship (1976-1983) for crimes against humanity — the first such trial in Latin America. Generals Videla and Massera received life sentences. Prosecutor Strassera's closing statement 'Nunca Más' (Never Again) became iconic. Subsequent 'Full Stop' (Punto Final) and 'Due Obedience' laws (1986-87) blocked lower-level prosecutions but were declared unconstitutional in 2003. By 2023, over 1,000 former military and police had been convicted.
laws.penalty: Crimes against humanity: life imprisonment (no statute of limitations). Crimes remain prosecutable regardless of amnesties declared unconstitutional.
exceptions: Full Stop and Due Obedience laws nullified — no amnesty available
Good behavior may affect prison conditions but not sentence length
Witnesses and justice collaborators receive protection

quiz.q: What phrase became iconic from Argentina's 1985 Trial of the Juntas?
quiz.explanation: Prosecutor Julio Strassera's closing statement ending with 'Señores jueces: Nunca Más' (Your Honors: Never Again) became one of the most powerful phrases in Argentine history. The phrase was adopted as the title of the national report on disappearances during the dictatorship, documenting over 30,000 victims.

laws.title: Default & Restructuring — Sovereign Debt Crisis
laws.subtitle: 2001-2002 default: world's largest at the time
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's 2001-2002 economic crisis led to the world's largest sovereign debt default at the time — $100 billion. The peso was devalued after being pegged to the dollar since 1991 (Convertibility Plan). The crisis caused 5 presidents in 2 weeks, riots, and 'que se vayan todos' (throw them all out) protests. Argentina conducted debt restructurings in 2005 and 2010 with 93% creditor participation. 'Holdout' creditors (vulture funds, led by NML Capital) obtained US court rulings blocking Argentina's debt payments until 2016.
laws.penalty: Sovereign default has no criminal penalties for the country itself, but triggers cross-default clauses in other bonds and blocks market access.
exceptions: IMF loans have special seniority treatment
Some bonds have collective action clauses (CACs) facilitating restructuring
Multilateral development bank loans generally cannot be restructured

quiz.q: Approximately how much was Argentina's 2001-2002 sovereign debt default?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 2001-2002 sovereign debt default was approximately $100 billion — the world's largest at the time. The crisis stemmed from maintaining a peso-dollar peg that made Argentine exports uncompetitive and led to unsustainable debt accumulation during the Convertibility era.

laws.title: Matrimonio Igualitario — Marriage Equality Law
laws.subtitle: Law 26.618 (2010) — first Latin American marriage equality
laws.fullDescription: Argentina became the first country in Latin America to legalize same-sex marriage nationally through Law 26.618 (July 2010) — making Argentina the 10th country globally. The law fully equalized marriage rights including adoption rights. The law passed the Senate 33-27 after a historic debate attended by thousands of supporters and opponents. Argentina's gender identity law (2012) allows gender marker changes without psychiatric diagnosis or surgery. Argentina also permits non-binary 'X' gender markers. Buenos Aires had recognized same-sex civil unions since 2002.
laws.penalty: Discrimination against same-sex couples by public officials: administrative sanctions, civil liability.
exceptions: Religious institutions may decline to perform ceremonies
Religious officiants retain freedom of conscience for ceremony performance
State civil registries must issue marriage certificates

quiz.q: Argentina became the first country in Latin America to legalize same-sex marriage nationally in what year?
quiz.explanation: Argentina legalized same-sex marriage nationally through Law 26.618 in July 2010, becoming the first country in Latin America and the 10th country globally to do so. The law fully equalized marriage rights including adoption, and was followed by a progressive 2012 gender identity law.

laws.title: Aborto Legal — Voluntary Interruption of Pregnancy
laws.subtitle: Law 27.610 (2021) — legal abortion up to 14 weeks
laws.fullDescription: Argentina legalized abortion on request up to 14 weeks through Law 27.610 (December 2020, signed January 2021) — one of the largest and most Catholic countries to do so. After abortion requests, the procedure must be performed within 10 days. Beyond 14 weeks, abortion remains legal for rape and health/life risk. Conscientious objection allowed for individual providers but not healthcare systems — a substitute provider must be guaranteed. The campaign for legalization (symbolized by the green handkerchief) ran for years and was also adopted internationally.
laws.penalty: Illegal abortion: only providers face sanctions, not patients. Refusal to provide legal abortion: civil liability, professional sanctions.
exceptions: Conscientious objection for individual providers requires a substitute
Public hospitals must guarantee access within the 10-day window
Minors can access services with or without parental consent (capacity-based)
laws.sourceLabel: Ministerio de Salud — Interrupción Voluntaria del Embarazo

quiz.q: Up to what gestational age does Argentina's Law 27.610 allow abortion on request?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Law 27.610 allows abortion on request up to 14 weeks of pregnancy. After 14 weeks, abortion remains legal for cases of rape or when necessary to protect the health or life of the pregnant person. The law requires healthcare providers to perform the procedure within 10 days of request.

laws.title: Glaciares — Glacier Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Law 26.639 (2010) — first national glacier protection
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Glacier Protection Law (Law 26.639, 2010) was the first national glacier protection law in the Americas. It prohibits all extractive activities (mining, oil, construction) in glaciers and periglacial environments. IANIGLA (Argentine Institute for Snow, Ice, and Environmental Research) conducts the National Glacier Inventory. Argentina holds 46% of South America's glaciated area, providing freshwater for arid regions. Mining companies (particularly Barrick Gold's Pascua-Lama project) challenged the law but courts upheld it.
laws.penalty: Activities in protected glaciers: immediate suspension, civil liability, criminal prosecution (2-5 years).
exceptions: Scientific research with permits
Activities predating the law continue under environment assessment
Small glaciers in extremely arid areas may have modified protection in some interpretations

quiz.q: What percentage of South America's glaciated area is found in Argentina?
quiz.explanation: Argentina holds approximately 46% of South America's glaciated area — critical freshwater reserves for arid and semi-arid regions including Mendoza's wine country. Argentina's Glacier Protection Law (2010) was the first in the Americas to prohibit mining, oil, and construction in glaciers and periglacial environments.

laws.title: Ley de Medios — Media Democratization
laws.subtitle: Audiovisual Communication Services Law 26.522 (2009)
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Ley de Medios (Law 26.522, 2009) limited media concentration, requiring divestiture of licenses that exceeded limits. It capped ownership at 10 broadcast licenses nationally, prohibited national networks from owning local affiliates beyond limits, and reserved 33% of broadcast spectrum for non-commercial entities. The law was heavily contested by Clarín Group. The Supreme Court upheld it in 2013. The Macri government issued emergency decrees (2015-2019) effectively gutting the concentration limits, which Fernández partially restored. Argentina's media landscape remains highly polarized.
laws.penalty: License violations: fines, license revocation. Concentration violations: forced divestiture orders.
exceptions: Public broadcaster (TV Pública, Radio Nacional) exempt from commercial limits
Community media have simplified license procedures
Foreign ownership of media limited under separate provisions

quiz.q: What percentage of broadcast spectrum does Argentina's Ley de Medios reserve for non-commercial entities?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Ley de Medios reserves 33% of broadcast spectrum for non-commercial entities — including community radio and TV stations, indigenous media, and civil society organizations. This was a central democratic provision, alongside concentration limits on commercial licenses.

laws.title: Retenciones — Agricultural Export Taxes
laws.subtitle: Export duties on soy, corn, and wheat
laws.fullDescription: Argentina taxes agricultural exports (retenciones) as a key revenue source and to keep domestic food prices lower. Soybean exports face duties of 30-33%, corn and wheat 12%. Argentine farmers (el campo) have repeatedly protested retenciones — most notably in the 2008 conflict (Resolución 125) when proposed sliding-scale soybean duties triggered a 4-month agricultural lockout. Argentina produces 50% of the world's sunflower oil and is a top 5 soybean exporter. AFIP administers export taxes which are paid in USD by exporters.
laws.penalty: Evasion of export duties: criminal prosecution under customs law, fines equal to 2x underpaid taxes.
exceptions: Regional wines and specialized agricultural products have differential rates
Biofuels derived from soybeans have separate duty framework
Small producers (below threshold) may have reduced rates

quiz.q: What duty does Argentina apply to soybean exports?
quiz.explanation: Argentina applies export duties (retenciones) of 30-33% on soybean exports — a major revenue source for the government and a mechanism to keep domestic food prices lower. The agricultural sector has repeatedly protested these duties, most famously in the 2008 conflict over the proposed sliding-scale Resolución 125.

laws.title: CONICET — Science and Research
laws.subtitle: National Scientific Research Council — public science
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's CONICET (Consejo Nacional de Investigaciones Científicas y Técnicas, 1958) is the primary national research institution, employing over 11,000 researchers across 300+ institutes. CONICET-affiliated institutions produced 90%+ of Argentina's scientific publications. Scientists receive CONICET fellowships and researcher positions (Carrera del Investigador). Brain drain ('fuga de cerebros') has been an ongoing concern — economic crises drive qualified scientists abroad. The Milei government (2023) proposed significant CONICET budget cuts, generating scientific community protests.
laws.penalty: CONICET research misconduct: internal disciplinary proceedings, funding revocation. Scientific fraud: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Researchers may have joint appointments with universities
International collaborative projects funded by foreign grants have modified reporting
Private sector CONICET partnerships operate under transfer agreements

quiz.q: How many researchers does Argentina's CONICET employ?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's CONICET employs over 11,000 researchers across 300+ institutes — making it one of Latin America's largest scientific research councils. CONICET-affiliated institutions produce over 90% of Argentina's scientific publications indexed in international databases.

laws.title: Asignación Universal por Hijo — Child Allowance
laws.subtitle: AUH — universal child allowance for informal workers
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Asignación Universal por Hijo (AUH), created by executive decree in 2009, provides a monthly allowance to unemployed and informal workers with children under 18, and to domestic employees. The AUH is conditional on school enrollment and vaccination. It covers approximately 4 million children. The benefit is automatically deducted — 80% paid monthly, 20% upon presenting health and education certificates. AUH is considered one of Latin America's most important social programs in reducing child poverty.
laws.penalty: Benefit fraud: repayment of received amounts, disqualification from AUH.
exceptions: Families with formal employment receive Family Allowances (Asignaciones Familiares) through ANSES instead
Children with disabilities receive enhanced AUH
Multiple children per family each receive the benefit

quiz.q: What percentage of AUH benefits are withheld monthly and released upon presenting school and health certificates?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's AUH pays 80% of the monthly allowance directly each month. The remaining 20% is withheld and released annually upon presenting certificates of school enrollment and vaccination compliance. This conditional structure aims to improve health and education outcomes for beneficiary children.

laws.title: Tránsito Nacional — Road Safety Law
laws.subtitle: Law 24.449 — national traffic law
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's National Traffic Law (Law 24.449) establishes traffic rules including maximum speeds (urban: 60 km/h, rural: 110 km/h, highways: 130 km/h), mandatory seatbelts, blood alcohol limit of 0.5g/L (0 for motorcyclists and commercial drivers), and compulsory vehicle technical inspection (VTV). Each province administers traffic enforcement. The ANSV (National Road Safety Agency) coordinates national campaigns. Argentina has approximately 5,000 traffic deaths annually — among Latin America's highest proportionally.
laws.penalty: Drunk driving (0.5-1.5g/L): fine + license suspension. Above 1.5g/L: criminal prosecution. Fatal accident while impaired: manslaughter charges.
exceptions: Zero BAC applies to motorcyclists, professional drivers, and those under 21
Emergency vehicles have different speed rules
Electric bicycles have modified classification
laws.sourceLabel: ANSV — Agencia Nacional de Seguridad Vial

quiz.q: What is the blood alcohol limit for motorcyclists driving in Argentina?
quiz.explanation: Argentina applies zero blood alcohol tolerance (0.0g/L) for motorcyclists, commercial drivers, and drivers under 21. The general limit for private car drivers is 0.5g/L. Exceeding 1.5g/L triggers criminal prosecution rather than just administrative penalties.

laws.title: BCRA — Central Bank and Peso Controls
laws.subtitle: Foreign exchange restrictions — cepo cambiario
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Central Bank (BCRA) periodically imposes strict foreign exchange controls ('cepo cambiario') to prevent capital flight and USD depletion. Under various administrations, Argentines face limits on USD purchases (historically $200/month), taxes on USD transactions (including 'blue chip swap'), and restrictions on profit remittances by companies. The official exchange rate often diverges from informal 'blue dollar' rates. The Milei government (2023) announced plans to dollarize the economy. Argentina's foreign reserves have frequently reached critically low levels.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized foreign currency transactions: BCRA fines, asset freezes. Black market currency trading: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Export earnings must be converted to pesos within timeframes
Tourism allowances for international travel
Essential imports may receive preferential exchange rates
laws.sourceLabel: Banco Central de la República Argentina

quiz.q: What colloquial term describes Argentina's informal foreign exchange market where dollars trade above the official rate?
quiz.explanation: The 'dólar blue' (blue dollar) refers to Argentina's informal/black market exchange rate for US dollars, which typically trades at a significant premium above the official BCRA exchange rate. The divergence between official and blue rates reflects capital controls and lack of confidence in the peso.

laws.title: Constitución de 1994 — Reformed Constitution
laws.subtitle: 1994 reform — reelection, human rights, autonomy
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's 1994 constitutional reform under President Menem enabled presidential re-election (previously prohibited) and extended the term to 4 years. Key additions: direct presidential election (ending the Electoral College), Buenos Aires City autonomy, constitutional status for international human rights treaties (making them paramount law alongside the Constitution), creation of the public ombudsman (Defensoría del Pueblo), and environmental rights. The 1994 reform also introduced the amparos (injunctions), habeas data, and habeas corpus as express constitutional mechanisms.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations by officials: impeachment, removal, criminal prosecution. International treaty violations: international legal proceedings.
exceptions: Constitutional reform requires special constituent assembly — can't be done by Congress alone
Some original 1853 constitutional provisions have extra protection
Provincial constitutions must align with national constitution

quiz.q: What major change regarding the presidency did Argentina's 1994 constitutional reform introduce?
options: It enabled presidential re-election and changed the term to 4 years
It extended the presidential term to 6 years
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 1994 constitutional reform (Pacto de Olivos between Menem and Alfonsín) enabled presidential re-election (previously prohibited) and changed the term from 6 years to 4 years with one re-election. It also established direct presidential election, eliminating the Electoral College.

laws.title: Identidad de Género — Gender Identity Law
laws.subtitle: Law 26.743 (2012) — landmark self-identification
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Gender Identity Law (Law 26.743, 2012) allows any person to change their registered gender and name without medical intervention, psychiatric diagnosis, or judicial proceedings — revolutionary globally when passed. The process is purely administrative (civil registry). Non-binary identities ('X' marker) were added by 2021 decree. Argentina's law inspired similar reforms in many countries. The law also guarantees access to gender-affirming healthcare through the public health system.
laws.penalty: Denial of gender marker change by civil registry: constitutional action (amparo). Discrimination against trans persons in employment/housing: civil liability.
exceptions: Minors require parental consent or judicial authorization
Non-binary marker 'X' available for all since 2021
Name change allowed regardless of gender change

quiz.q: What made Argentina's 2012 Gender Identity Law revolutionary when passed?
options: It was the first law allowing any gender change
It allowed gender change without medical intervention, diagnosis, or judicial proceedings
It created special protections for intersex persons
It guaranteed trans persons priority in public employment
quiz.explanation: Argentina's 2012 Gender Identity Law was revolutionary because it allowed gender marker and name changes through a purely administrative process — no psychiatric diagnosis, no medical treatment, and no judicial proceeding required. This self-identification approach inspired similar laws in many other countries.

laws.title: Ley de Bosques — Native Forest Protection
laws.subtitle: Law 26.331 (2007) — deforestation moratorium and zoning
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Native Forest Law (Law 26.331, 2007) required all provinces to map their forests into three categories: red (no clearing permitted), yellow (restricted use with environmental impact assessment), and green (clearing permitted with limitations). It established a national fund for forest conservation. Argentina had lost 70% of its native forests before the law. Implementation has been inconsistent — Chaco, Salta, and Santiago del Estero continued significant deforestation. Argentina committed to zero deforestation in the Paris Agreement context.
laws.penalty: Illegal deforestation: fines up to $1 million ARS, reforestation obligation, criminal prosecution (2-5 years).
exceptions: Limited clearing in 'yellow' zones with environmental impact assessment
Small subsistence farming has reduced requirements
Existing forest concessions have transition provisions

quiz.q: Argentina's Native Forest Law categorizes forests into how many protection categories?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Law 26.331 categorizes native forests into three categories using a traffic light system: Red (no clearing — highest conservation value), Yellow (restricted use requiring environmental impact assessment), and Green (clearing permitted with limitations). Provinces must map their forests accordingly.

laws.title: Producción Pública de Medicamentos
laws.subtitle: Public pharmaceutical manufacturing — affordable medicines
laws.fullDescription: Argentina has a robust public pharmaceutical manufacturing sector, unique in Latin America. Provincial laboratories (Laboratorio Industrial Farmacéutico de Santa Fe, LAFORMED, etc.) produce essential medicines distributed free through the public health system. The National Medicines, Food and Medical Technology Administration (ANMAT) regulates all medicines. Argentina's pharmaceutical industry is among Latin America's most developed, with significant generic production. Compulsory licensing provisions allow generic production of patented medicines for public health emergencies.
laws.penalty: Marketing unapproved medicines: ANMAT sanctions, fines, confiscation. Counterfeit medicines: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: ANMAT emergency authorization for novel treatments
Compulsory licensing during health emergencies
Homeopathic and traditional medicines have simplified registration

quiz.q: What distinguishes Argentina's public pharmaceutical sector from most Latin American countries?
options: Argentina has extensive public laboratories manufacturing essential medicines
Argentina bans all foreign pharmaceutical companies
Argentina has the highest medicine prices in Latin America
quiz.explanation: Argentina has a relatively large network of provincial public pharmaceutical laboratories (including LAFORMED and others) that manufacture essential medicines distributed free through the public health system. This public manufacturing capacity is unusual in Latin America and provides some buffer against price pressures from private manufacturers.

laws.title: Código Penal — Criminal Code Reforms
laws.subtitle: Femicide, digital crimes, and preventive detention
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Penal Code has been significantly updated in recent decades. Law 26.791 (2012) introduced femicide as an aggravated homicide category (life imprisonment). Law 26.388 (2008) criminalized computer crimes including unauthorized access, data interception, and digital fraud. Preventive detention is broadly used — over 50% of Argentina's prison population is in pretrial detention. Prison overcrowding is severe, and the Supreme Court has issued emergency orders. The 'flagrancia' procedure (for caught-in-the-act crimes) allows expedited trials within 90 days.
laws.penalty: Femicide: life imprisonment. Computer crimes: 15 days-3 years. Aggravated robbery: 6-15 years.
exceptions: Minors tried under separate juvenile justice framework
Mental incapacity may affect criminal responsibility
Suspended sentences for first offenses under 3 years

quiz.q: What criminal innovation did Argentina's Law 26.791 (2012) introduce to the Penal Code?
options: Femicide as an aggravated homicide category
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Law 26.791 (2012) introduced femicide — the murder of a woman by a man motivated by gender-based violence — as an aggravated category of homicide carrying a life sentence. Argentina was one of the early Latin American countries to legislate femicide following the Ni Una Menos movement.

laws.title: Ley de Educación Nacional — Public Education
laws.subtitle: Law 26.206 (2006) — 13 years mandatory education
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's National Education Law (Law 26.206, 2006) extended compulsory education from 10 to 13 years (from pre-school through secondary). It guarantees free public education at all levels including university. The National University Law (Law 24.521) confirms tuition-free and autonomous public universities. Argentina has 130 national universities serving over 2 million students. University autonomy means national government cannot enter campuses without rector's permission. Argentina's literacy rate is 99% — among Latin America's highest.
laws.penalty: States failing to provide free compulsory education: constitutional obligations enforceable. School dropout intervention: social services referral.
exceptions: Private universities may charge tuition and operate under separate registration
Religious schools receive state subsidies but maintain curricular autonomy
Indigenous education has bilingual intercultural provisions

quiz.q: How many years of compulsory education does Argentina's 2006 National Education Law require?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's National Education Law (2006) extended compulsory education to 13 years — from pre-primary (4-5 years old) through the completion of secondary school. This extended the previous 10-year requirement and placed Argentina among the countries with the most extensive compulsory education in Latin America.

laws.title: Precios Cuidados — Price Controls
laws.subtitle: Monitored prices program for basic goods
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Precios Cuidados program (launched 2014, periodically modified) establishes agreed maximum prices for a basket of essential consumer goods (food, hygiene, cleaning products) sold in major supermarkets. Prices are negotiated between the Secretariat of Commerce and manufacturers/retailers. The program aims to control inflation — Argentina has experienced among the world's highest inflation rates, exceeding 200% in 2023. Companies that violate the agreed prices face administrative fines. Consumers can report violations through the SECOM app.
laws.penalty: Violating Precios Cuidados: administrative fines, publication on 'blacklist' of violating companies.
exceptions: Small independent supermarkets have modified participation rules
Regional products may have adjusted prices
Export versions of products not subject to domestic price controls

quiz.q: Approximately what was Argentina's annual inflation rate in 2023, one of the highest globally?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's inflation exceeded 200% annually in 2023 — one of the highest rates in the world. This extreme inflation context makes price control programs like Precios Cuidados politically important, though economists debate their effectiveness in controlling underlying inflation.

laws.title: Corte Suprema — Supreme Court Composition
laws.subtitle: 5-member Supreme Court — political appointments
laws.fullDescription: Argentina's Supreme Court of Justice (Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación) has 5 justices appointed by the President with Senate confirmation. The court has had 9 members for periods when expanded by Menem (1990) and Kirchner (reduced to 5 in 2006). The court's composition is politically sensitive — several governments have attempted to expand or modify it. The Milei government (2023) announced a proposal to expand to 25 members. The court is the final interpreter of Argentina's Constitution and has issued landmark rulings on human rights, media, and federal-provincial relations.
laws.penalty: Failure to comply with Supreme Court rulings: contempt proceedings. Judicial corruption: criminal prosecution and removal.
exceptions: Constitutional reform requires constituent assembly — court composition by simple law
Justices serve until voluntary retirement or age 75 without reconfirmation
Impeachment requires 2/3 Senate majority
laws.sourceLabel: Corte Suprema de Justicia de la Nación

quiz.q: How many justices currently serve on Argentina's Supreme Court?
quiz.explanation: Argentina's Supreme Court currently has 5 justices, after being reduced from 9 members in 2006 under Kirchner. Each justice is appointed by the President with Senate confirmation and serves until voluntary retirement or age 75.

laws.title: AFA — Football and Society
laws.subtitle: Argentine Football Association — football as national religion
laws.fullDescription: Football is deeply embedded in Argentina's national identity. The AFA (Asociación del Fútbol Argentino, 1893) governs Argentine football, which produced legendary players including Diego Maradona and Lionel Messi. Argentina won the 2022 World Cup, triggering massive national celebrations. Clubs like River Plate and Boca Juniors are as much social and cultural institutions as sports clubs. Football violence (barras bravas) is regulated by Law 24.192 with criminal penalties. The Nacional B and Primera División are the top leagues.
laws.penalty: Football stadium violence: 3-10 years imprisonment under Law 24.192. Clubs can be disqualified and fined for supporter violence.
exceptions: Children's football leagues have separate governance
Amateur football under AFA affiliated leagues has different rules
International competitions governed by FIFA/CONMEBOL rules

quiz.q: In what year did Argentina win the FIFA World Cup most recently?
quiz.explanation: Argentina won the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar, defeating France in a dramatic penalty shootout final. It was Argentina's third World Cup title and Lionel Messi's first, after winning in 1978 and 1986. The victory triggered one of the largest celebrations in Argentine history.
